On Jan. 1, 2027, a temporary increase in fees for electronic access to court records will take effect to help reimburse the costs of the development of the new case management and public access system. 

The increase of two cents per page, from 10 cents to 12 cents, was approved by the Judicial Conference’s Executive Committee on behalf of the Judicial Conference of the United States. The department’s Wage and Hour Division investigators determined the employer also failed to pay minimum wage for all hours worked and maintain required records, all in violation of the Fair Labor Standards Act.Federal recordkeeping regulations require employers to keep records for each employee covered by the FLSA, including identification details, hours worked, and the wages earned.Workers and employers can call the Wage and Hour Division with questions and requests for compliance assistance at its toll-free helpline, 866-4US-WAGE (487-9243). Employers are encouraged to use the agency’s industry-specific compliance assistance toolkits to learn about their responsibilities under the laws enforced by the division. The agency’s PAID program offers employers an opportunity to self-report and resolve potential minimum wage and overtime violations under the FLSA, as well as certain potential violations under the Family and Medical Leave Act. Learn more about the Wage and Hour Division, including a search tool that workers can use if they think they may be owed back wages collected by the division. Looking Ahead: Eligibility-Dedicated Data Feed to Support MaineCare Renewals and Enrollment

Sep 04, 2026

Two weeks ago, we announced communications support for MaineCare partners and providers regarding changes the federal government is making to MaineCare (Maine’s Medicaid program) eligibility. This message provides an early look at planned data-sharing that will help the Maine Department of Health and Human Services (DHHS) verify information needed for MaineCare eligibility. Our goal is to help eligible Mainers keep their coverage and access to services with as little disruption as possible.

No action is needed now. We are sharing this information early to make providers aware of what is being planned. We will share more information as plans and timelines are finalized.

DHHS will continue to use administrative data sources it has access to as much as possible to support automatic (“passive”) renewals for MaineCare members. Federal changes to eligibility mean we need additional information to help more eligible members maintain their MaineCare coverage. This data will help Mainers continue to benefit from MaineCare, which in turn will help providers minimize the impact of these federal Medicaid cuts on their revenue and on their charity and uncompensated care.

Clinical Data Will Help People Stay Enrolled in MaineCare

Electronic health record (EHR) systems contain clinical data that Maine and numerous other states are planning to use to help exempt Medicaid applicants and members with work-limiting health conditions from Work Requirements. In Maine, this data will support MaineCare eligibility determination activities administered by the Office for Family Independence (OFI). DHHS intends to partner with providers to collect this information through HealthInfoNet, the State’s contractor for this work. HealthInfoNet will identify indicators of exemptions from work requirements by collecting and processing this clinical data from providers. Using clinical data alongside claims and other administrative data to generate more timely and comprehensive information will help keep Mainers enrolled in MaineCare. We will refer to the data sent to HealthInfoNet for this purpose as the eligibility-dedicated clinical data feed.

Until the eligibility-dedicated clinical data feed is established we will be basing automatic exceptions for work-limiting health conditions on claims data alone in order to meet implementation deadlines.

This Data Sharing Will Be Separate from the Health Information Exchange

The eligibility-dedicated clinical data feed will be separate from the health information exchange (HIE) data that many providers already share with HealthInfoNet.

The eligibility-dedicated data feed will include only the information needed to support MaineCare eligibility activities. This information will be stored separately from HIE data. It will not be available through HealthInfoNet’s clinical portal or through analytics tools used by some provider organizations. The eligibility-dedicated clinical data feed will be used only in support of OMS and OFI activities associated with eligibility.

Key details to note:

  • The steps needed for a provider to establish this new data feed will vary by provider organization. For example, some provider organizations already have a data feed with HealthInfoNet that can be used as a starting point. Capabilities of the organization’s EHR vendor or technology support may also affect the work needed to establish the data feed. Providers eligible for relevant Rural Health Transformation Program (RHTP) funding may consider using this funding for these costs, as determined by the allowable uses of specific RHTP opportunities.
  • We expect it will take the majority of provider organizations two to four months to build their eligibility-dedicated clinical data feed with HealthInfoNet. This time range will be dependent on provider organization’s or vendor’s availability to engage with HealthInfoNet. We expect it will take less time than building a typical HIE data sharing connection with HealthInfoNet.
  • Clinical care teams are not expected to need to take additional steps to send this information as part of their day-to-day work. Once the data feed is established, the identified data categories will be shared automatically with HealthInfoNet.
  • Broad categories of exemptions in statute for work-limiting health conditions include those who are blind or disabled, have a substance use disorder, disabling mental disorder, or complex medical condition. DHHS continues to work with the federal government to clarify data related to these categories that may assist states to automatically exempt individuals, including information related to a person’s ability to work. Kinds of data may include demographic information, diagnosis indicators, encounter or event indicators, and billing codes, among others.

More Information Will Be Coming – No Action Needed Now The Department and HealthInfoNet will distribute instructions for provider organizations to opt into this initiative and implement the eligibility-dedicated data feed. Future communications will include information such as:

  • Which provider types will be prioritized for establishing these connections
  • How providers can participate
  • The types of information that will be needed
  • Technical requirements and specifications
  • Onboarding and implementation steps

entry.title: Updates to the National Pollutant Discharge Elimination System Definitions and Exclusions — Federal Register — Documents Matching 'Maine'
entry.content: The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) proposes to revise a regulatory definition under the Clean Water Act (CWA) permitting regulations pertaining to discharges in the contiguous zone and ocean. The proposal would revise the regulatory definition of "discharge of a pollutant" to reflect and faithfully implement the statutory exclusion of vessels and other floating craft that add pollutants in the contiguous zone or the ocean from inclusion in the definition of "discharge of a pollutant" or "discharge", and thus, from National Pollutant Discharge Elimination System (NPDES) program requirements. The proposed rulemaking would also make conforming and clarifying changes to the NPDES regulatory exclusion for vessels and other floating craft. The effect of these changes would be that the addition of pollutants by a vessel or other floating craft in the contiguous zone or the ocean that is not secured to the seabed would not be a discharge and would not require CWA NPDES permit authorization to add pollutants to those waters.

entry.title: General Election is two months away; Secretary of State’s Office provides update on Maine election processes — Maine Secretary of State — Bureau of Corporations, Elections & Commissions News
entry.content:
AUGUSTA, MAINE – Today September 4, marks just 60 days until the General Election on November 3. The Office of the Secretary of State today provided an update about Maine’s election processes for this stage of the election cycle.

Key dates to know:

  • September 15 - National Voter Registration Day
  • September 19 (45 days before Election Day) - Deadline to send UOCAVA ballots to already pending requests
  • October 4 (30 days before Election Day) - In-person, no-excuse absentee voting period begins (goes through close of business in a voter's town on Thurs., October 29)
  • October 20 - Election Hero Day
  • October 27 - Mock Election Day
  • October 29 - Last day to request a no-excuse absentee ballot
  • Registration deadlines:
    • In person: Close of the polls on Election Day.
    • Registering by mail or 3rd person: Received by the voter’s town or city by close of business 21 days before Election Day. (October 13) 
    • Registering online: 5 PM on the 21st day before Election Day. (October 13)
    • Registration through the BMV: On the 7th day before Election Day. (October 27)
    • UOCAVA voters in Title 21-A section 777-A by mail or electronically: By Noon the day before Election Day (November 2)
  • Absentee ballots:
    • Requesting an absentee ballot: Absentee ballots, including accessible ballots and ballots for uniformed and overseas voters, may be requested online at maine.gov/cgi-bin/online/AbsenteeBallot/index.pl. Voters may also contact their town hall to request a ballot or submit a paper application for an absentee ballot, and the request must be received at least three business days before Election Day (October 29), unless special circumstances exist.
    • Returning an absentee ballot: Only ballots received by 8 p.m. on Election Day are counted, regardless of postmark. In many towns and cities, voters have the option of returning an absentee ballot to a secured drop box. Maine voters can track the process of their ballot at: apps.web.maine.gov/cgi-bin/online/AbsenteeBallot/ballot_status.pl.

Absentee ballot processing

Absentee ballots may be processed up to seven days before Election Day, with notice provided to the Secretary of State and political parties 30 days before Election Day. A list of municipalities which may process ballots early will be available at maine.gov/sos/elections-voting/upcoming-elections at least one week prior to the start of early processing. Absentee ballot processing is a public process which may be observed by partisan and nonpartisan observers. Early processing may happen between the hours of 7 a.m. and 9 p.m., except when an inspection is requested. At such times, processing may not begin until the inspection period has concluded. Requests for inspection of absentee ballot applications and envelopes must be submitted in writing by 4 p.m. the day before each day of early processing. If such a request is made, the ballot applications and envelopes will be available an hour before early processing is set to begin.

During absentee ballot processing, teams of two work in stages. First, the absentee voter list is marked, then the ballots and envelopes separated, and only when a sufficient quantity of ballots has amassed, are the ballots unfolded and placed into the tabulator or ballot box. Ballots and envelopes are kept secure after each day of early processing. Absentee ballots are not counted until after 8 p.m. on Election Day, just as all other ballots. Many municipalities will conduct absentee ballot processing on Election Day itself, under the same procedures. 

Ranked-Choice Voting

With declared write-in candidates in both the U.S. Senate and the Congressional District 2 races, those races will be conducted by ranked choice. The ballots will include the names of the nominees as well as a blank write-in line with columns to rank candidate preferences. The list of declared write-in candidates is posted on the Secretary of State website and will be posted in polling locations. 

Ranked-choice voting, sometimes called "instant run-off voting," allows voters to choose their candidate(s) in order of preference, by marking candidates as their first, second and/or third choice. Voters may rank as many or as few candidates as they choose. 

In ranked-choice races, to win the race outright, a candidate must receive more than 50% of the first-choice votes as counted on Election Day. If no candidate receives 50% plus one vote of the total ballots cast in a particular race, then the tabulation will proceed to Augusta for the ranked-choice tabulation. The votes are tabulated in rounds, with the lowest-ranked candidates eliminated in each round until a remaining candidate receives a majority of the votes (more than 50%). The candidate who is determined to have received the majority of the votes (more than 50%) in the final round is declared the winner. entry.title: New counsel memo: Standard of review for Right-to-Sue requests made before 180 days have passed — Maine Human Rights Commission — Latest News
entry.content:
MEMO TO: Kit Thomson Crossman, Executive Director FROM: Barbara Archer Hirsch, Commission Counsel Colin R. Hurd, Deputy Commission Counsel DATE: July 23, 2025 RE: Standard of review for right-to-sue requests made before 180 days have passed As you are aware, 5 M.R.S. § 4612(6)(B), enacted in 2023, delineates the circumstances in which the Executive Director (“ED”) shall issue a right-to-sue letter (“RTS”) to a complainant who requests one before their complaint has aged 180 days with the Commission. Prior to the 2023 enactment, complainants could never request an RTS prior to 180 days. Now, the Commission “shall” issue an early RTS when two elements are concurrently met. First, the ED must determine that the complainant demonstrated good cause for requesting the RTS before the passage of 180 days, and second, the ED must certify that it is probable that the Commission will be unable to conclude its investigation before the 180 th day from the date on which the complaint was filed. After 180 days have passed, the complainant may request and receive an RTS without having to meet these standards. The second element of § 4612(6)(B) is relatively straightforward. The first element, however, is more nuanced. The Maine Human Rights Act does not define “good cause”. The Commission’s Procedural Rule provides that the Commission may grant extensions of certain time limits “for good cause shown”, 94-348 C.M.R. Ch. 2, § 2.11(C), but also do not define the term. In practice, the Commission requires that parties seeking extensions demonstrate that the requested extension is necessary due to extenuating circumstances, such as serious personal illness or a death in the family; inconvenience is insufficient to meet this standard.

entry.title: Trump’s Trade War with Canada is Not Maine’s — Governor of Maine — Newsroom Press Releases
entry.content:
Hello, this is Governor Janet Mills, and thank you for listening.

You know, last summer I sat down for a cup of coffee at Tim Hortons in Caribou with Ron Turcotte, the legendary jockey who rode Secretariat to the Triple Crown in 1973. Ron Turcotte lived across the border in New Brunswick, Canada, but he picked up his mail at the U.S. Post Office in Van Buren, Maine, and did errands there.

His life showcased the reality of so many people living along the Maine-Canadian border. Yeah, there may be an international border there, but our communities, families, and economies are deeply entwined. And in places like the Saint John Valley, these connections existed long before the border ever did.

Throughout Maine, the President's trade war has driven up the cost of everything from groceries to cars and trucks and construction materials we need to build more homes. Because these tariffs are nothing more than taxes on American families and businesses.

Now the President has escalated his trade war, imposing 50 percent tariffs on many Canadian goods. And life is about to get more expensive and more complicated for Maine people, as well as Canadians.

In the Saint John Valley, about 90 percent of municipal road salt comes from Canada. And now, because of the President's new taxes, a major Canadian distributor has announced that it will halt deliveries of salt for the foreseeable future. It's not unheard of for The County to see snow in late September or early October, so this isn't some abstract trade war—the President's reckless behavior may soon threaten public safety.

And the damage to our state from the President's arbitrary and whiplash tariffs is not limited to business with Canada. In 2024, a developer wanted to create 125 new jobs in Jay, Maine, by turning that shuttered paper mill into an oriented strand board manufacturing facility. But the President's tariffs then increased the cost of importing specialized equipment from Europe so that developer was forced to scrap his plans.

President Trump claims his tariffs will bring manufacturing jobs back to America, but hey in Jay, his tariffs killed 125 of those jobs before they could even be created.

Now Canada is responding to the recent tariffs with tariffs of their own. Soon they'll add taxes to goods that last year made up $170 million of Maine's exports. These tariffs will make exporting these goods more expensive—hurting industries and communities that never asked to be caught in this fight. Industries and communities that, like Ron Turcotte's life, just do not fit neatly on one side of the border or the other.

As I record this, negotiators have not reached an agreement to avoid Canada's retaliatory tariffs from taking effect on September 8th. President Trump must de-escalate this ridiculous trade war before his recklessness does any more damage to the world economy and to Maine's economy.

We in Maine know that we share more than a border with Canada. We share an economy, a history. We share friendships and families and a way of life. Our relationship does not belong to any one president or one prime minister. It belongs to the everyday Mainers and Canadians who can pull up a chair at Tim Hortons, do business together, be friends, and lend a hand when a neighbor needs one.

This is Governor Janet Mills, and thank you for listening.

entry.content: WASHINGTON – As America celebrates Labor Day and its 250th anniversary, the U.S. Department of Labor is honoring the generations of American workers whose skill, strength, ingenuity, and determination built the greatest nation and most powerful economy the world has ever known.For 250 years, American workers have built our cities, cultivated our land, powered our factories, forged our steel, laid our railroads, pioneered new technologies, and carried American industry to every corner of the globe. From the workshops and farms of 1776 to the factories, construction sites, small businesses, and cutting-edge industries of today, the American worker has always been the backbone of our nation.“American workers are the greatest workers in the world,” said Acting Secretary of Labor Keith Sonderling. “For 250 years, their skill, ingenuity, determination, and hard work have built the greatest nation and most powerful economy the world has ever known. This Labor Day, we celebrate the American workers, job creators, retirees, and unions who have built, manufactured, invented, and always outwork the rest of the world and who will lead America into its next 250 years.”Today, more Americans are working than at any point in the nation’s history. The unemployment rate remains below the historic average. The economy has added more than 1 million private sector jobs since President Trump took office, 401(k)s have reached record highs, and the U.S. manufacturing sector has expanded for eight straight months.President Trump has secured trillions of dollars in new investments, bringing jobs and high-skilled, high-paying opportunities back to communities across the country. At the Department of Labor, we are ensuring American workers have the skills to fill those jobs by expanding apprenticeships and skills-based training and preparing the next generation for the good-paying careers these investments are creating.This Labor Day, we celebrate the American workers and job creators who built the greatest economy in the world and encourage all Americans to pause, reflect, and recommit to ensuring the American worker remains our nation’s greatest asset.

Sep 08, 2026

As previously communicated, the Office of MaineCare Services (OMS) is preparing to launch an upgraded version of MIHMS, MaineCare’s claims processing system. The upgrade is currently scheduled to go live on October 10, 2026. To support a smooth transition, OMS must implement temporary system access limitations and adjustments to payment cycles in October.  

From Friday, October 2 at 8:00 PM until Monday, October 12 at 8:00 AM, MIHMS will be in a “data freeze” while OMS completes final system readiness and transition activities. 

Please note that we have updated the FAQ previously shared, as of September 8, 2026.

We strongly encourage providers to submit claims approaching timely filing limits in the next few weeks to avoid potential submission delays. The planned data freeze does not modify existing Medicaid timely filing requirements. Providers remain responsible for ensuring claims are submitted within the established timely filing guidelines.

We have previously shared that a refreshed and upgraded MIHMS, with a new “MaineCare Partner Portal,” is coming in October 2026. This will replace the current HealthPAS Online Portal. We are now inviting trading partners to register for training that begins September 8, 2026 to help you prepare for the transition to the new portal. Trading partners include providers, billing agents, health plans, clearinghouses, and business associates. Trading partners have an important role to play in supporting a smooth transition and uninterrupted access to the portal after go-live. 

Gainwell Technologies will be leading live virtual instructor-led training sessions. These courses will provide the knowledge and skills needed to navigate the new portal, complete daily business functions, and use new portal features. Training demonstrations, materials, and supporting resources will help participants prepare for a successful transition. 

Steps you need to take to attend training 

  • Review the available training topics listed below and identify the sessions that align with your role and responsibilities. 
  • Use the LMS registration (instructions below) to create an account, access the training catalog, and enroll in applicable sessions. 
  • Contact Gainwell (instructions below) if you need assistance. 
  • Recorded sessions and other training materials will be available in the LMS after training sessions for ongoing reference. 

MaineCare Partner Portal Training Sessions 

Course Name 

Description

Learn how to complete first-time login activities, configure multi-factor authentication (MFA), manage user accounts and permissions, perform account maintenance activities, and understand electronic data interchange (EDI) certification requirements and status monitoring. This course is only for Admin (R7) users.

MaineCare Telehealth Services Provider Licensure Requirements

Sep 08, 2026

As a reminder, all providers delivering telehealth services to MaineCare members must be enrolled with MaineCare and must comply with MaineCare Benefits Manual (MBM) Chapter I, Section 4: Telehealth Services.  

Chapter I, Section 4 requires that providers be “appropriately licensed, accredited, certified, and/or registered in the state where the member is located during the provision of the telehealth service.”  

This means that all providers delivering in-person or telehealth services to MaineCare members, who are in Maine at the time of the service, must hold appropriate Maine credentials or Interstate Licensure Compacts recognized by the Department of Professional and Financial Regulation (DPFR) or other appropriate organization.   

Pursuant to MBM, Ch. I, Section 1.18 failure to comply with these requirements can result in the denial of claims or recoupment of payment because services delivered without proper state licensure are not eligible for reimbursement. 

For questions, please contact your Provider Relations Specialist.

entry.title: US Department of Labor unveils agency-wide initiatives supporting American workers, job creators, retirees — U.S. Department of Labor — News Releases
entry.content: WASHINGTON – The U.S. Department of Labor today announced its latest round of opinion letters and ongoing policy efforts to provide greater guidance and transparency to support American workers, job creators, and retirees.“This Labor Day, the Department of Labor is providing all of its stakeholders with greater clarity on federal labor laws,” said Acting Secretary of Labor Keith Sonderling. “This Administration is committed to clear, practical compliance assistance that helps workers understand their rights, helps employers understand their obligations, and gives all stakeholders the certainty they need to comply with the law. In honor of Labor Day, 10 agencies across the Department of Labor are delivering on that commitment.”Learn more about the department’s initiatives on the Labor Day 2026 page.Center For Faith:The department’s Center for Faith created a resource to answer common questions that faith-based organizations have regarding federal wage and hour laws. Employee Benefits Security Administration: EBSA issued an advisory opinion considering whether the Blue and Gold Automotive Health Trust Fund Welfare Benefit Plan constitutes a viable association health plan under the Employee Retirement Income Security Act such that the employers involved can band together to obtain more favorable healthcare pricing options for their employees. EBSA also published a field assistance bulletin outlining the guiding principles for EBSA’s enforcement policy regarding the Mental Health Parity and Addiction Equity Act to focus resources on areas that will have the greatest impact on access to mental health and substance use disorder benefits.Employment and Training Administration:ETA released a Training and Employment Notice 05-26, establishing a five-component framework for effective pre-apprenticeships. By strengthening pre-apprenticeship programs and giving employers the guidance and tools necessary to funnel younger workers into registered apprenticeship programs, the Trump Administration is ensuring the American workforce gains and maintains the skills necessary to build the modern and future economy. ETA also issued Circular 2026-04, informing employers that sponsor registered apprentices how to obtain money made available through the new Workforce Pell Grant, created by the Working Families Tax Cuts Act. By following this guidance and partnering with eligible educational institutions, employers using registered apprentices can access program flexibilities that allow businesses to grow and apprentices to build a high-paying career in their communities.ETA published Unemployment Insurance Program Letter 14-26, furthering President Trump’s directive to fight fraud by setting expectations for state workforce agencies to develop and implement plans to combat fraud in their state-level unemployment insurance systems and clarifying when states must adopt corrective action plans for failure to protect against the misuse of American’s tax dollars. Bureau of International Labor Affairs:ILAB released videos highlighting the American stories that put our workers front and center. From shrimpers on the Gulf Coast to workers in Alaska powering our critical minerals supply chains, the recordings demonstrate how unfair foreign competition driven by labor abuse undercuts U.S. industries – and what a level playing field really looks like. Each story makes it clear President Trump’s work is increasing U.S. job and wage growth, enforcing fair labor standards, and backing American workers and businesses with the tools they need to compete and win.Mine Safety and Health Administration:Aiming to achieve greater consistency of outcomes, MSHA recently centralized its negotiators into the Conference Litigation and Investigative Resources group. This new structure will streamline conferences, reduce litigation costs, and enhance agency credibility before judges, operators, and miners. This will help support the Trump administration’s reinvigoration of the American coal industry.MSHA recently launched a new, comprehensive “professionalism” training course for inspectors, as well as managers and administrative staff in the field who also interact with the public. To best protect America’s crucial mine workforce, MSHA must earn the trust of and build lasting relationships with those who work in and operate American mines. Equipping MSHA investigators with the skills to do both is essential for rebuilding American mining dominance.Office of Labor-Management Standards:OLMS issued an advisory opinion letter considering whether a newly formed union’s initial officer selection process is subject to the election protections and requirements of Title IV of the Labor-Management Reporting and Disclosure Act. Occupational Safety and Health Administration:OSHA’s Voluntary Protection Programs promote effective worksite-based safety and health by recognizing employers for their achievements leading the way in creating stronger and safer worksites every day. OSHA recognizes employers and employees who have achieved exemplary occupational safety and health management systems through VPP.Wage and Hour Division: The division released three opinion letters responding to important questions on the application of the Fair Labor Standards Act: FLSA 2026-11: Whether an uncompensated 60-minute lunch break, during which employees spend six to 14 minutes walking to and from the employer’s designated break area, constitutes a bona fide meal period. FLSA 2026-12: Whether FLSA-exempt employees of a nonprofit organization may volunteer, outside of their normal work hours, to perform services for their employing organization.FLSA 2026-13: Whether the FLSA allows a restaurant supervisor who also works as a bartender to keep a portion of other employees’ tips and the extent to which he or she may participate in a tip pool.The Wage and Hour Division also updated its mobile app timesheet, now called WorkWise Timesheet, to provide streamlined tools for tracking regular work hours, breaks, overtime, and pay for both employees and employers.Office of Disability Employment Policy:ODEP unveiled the Make Work Pay Hub, a new website that helps job seekers, workers, retirees, and employers find financial planning resources for people with disabilities. The Hub features ABLE accounts, which let eligible workers save for disability-related expenses without affecting federal benefits, and Trump accounts, new tax-advantaged savings accounts for any U.S. citizen under 18.Veterans’ Employment and Training Service:VETS issued an opinion letter considering whether the Uniformed Services Employment and Reemployment Rights Act protects employees from any retaliatory action by their employers because they engaged in USERRA-protected activity.

Annual Tea Celebrating Deaf Culture to Take Place September 17

September 8, 2026

FOR IMMEDIATE RELEASE: September 8, 2026

Contact: Terry Morrell 470-7668 (videophone); 711 Maine Relay

Annual Tea Celebrating Deaf Culture to Take Place September 17

The 35th annual tea and awards presentation will take place from 2 to 4 p.m. in the Hall of Flags

AUGUSTA, MAINE -In celebration of Deaf culture and the heritage of AmericanSign Language (ASL), as well as Deaf literature, art and folklore, Governor Janet Mills has issued a proclamation designating the week of Sept. 20-26, 2026, as Deaf Culture Week.

To kick off the week, the Commission for the Deaf, Hard of Hearing and Late Deafened will hold its 35th Annual Tea in Celebration of Deaf Culture Week on Sept. 17, from 2 to 4 p.m. at the Hall of Flags in the State House in Augusta. The event is open to the public.

Clayton Marr III will give the keynote address. Marr grew up in Westbrook and currently lives in Knoxville, Tenn. where he is the student activity coordinator for the Tennessee Schools for the Deaf. He works with Deaf students to support their academic success, personal growth, and independence.

"Maine's Deaf community has enriched our state for generations through its language, culture, traditions and contributions. I've proudly declared September 20-26 as Deaf Culture Week in celebration of that heritage and the Deaf and hard-of-hearing Mainers who make our state a better place," said Governor Mills.

"The Maine Department of Labor is proud to support the Commission for the Deaf, Hard of Hearing and Late Deafened and this 35th annual celebration of Deaf culture. I encourage Maine employers to harness the many skills and experiences of people with disabilities. DOL's Bureau of Rehabilitation Services is ready to assist workers and employers with vocational rehabilitation, training and support," said Commissioner Laura Fortman.

This year, the Commission will present seven awards to eight individuals and organizations that have contributed to Deaf culture in Maine.

Awards and their recipients are:

Promoting American Sign Language, Deaf Culture and Deaf People Award Lisa Penney, Donna Van Horn

Citizenship Youth Award Gavin Phelan

Ginny Hewes Advocate for the Needs of the Deaf Community Award Jennifer McCann, LCSW

Outstanding Citizenship Award Andrew Blethen

Outstanding Commendation Award Immigrant Legal Advocacy Project (ILAP)

Dr. Toni H. Rees Interpreter Award Cid Pollard

Clifton F. Rodgers Outstanding Service to the Deaf Community Award Sammy Hargis

The Division of the Deaf, Hard of Hearing and Late Deafened, within the Bureau of Rehabilitation Services in the Maine Department of Labor, works to promote full access to employment, independence and community integration for people who are deaf or hard of hearing.

Maine Heads to The Big E with Food, Farms, and Makers

September 3, 2026

The Maine Building at the Big E returns for 17 days of Maine food, farms, makers, and traditions, September 18 - October 4

AUGUSTA, Maine (September 3, 2026) - From loaded Maine baked potatoes and lobster rolls to wild blueberry crisp, maple milkshakes, smoked salmon, and wood-fired pizza featuring Maine ingredients, the tastes and traditions of Maine are returning to The Big E this fall.

The State of Maine Building, located on the Avenue of States alongside buildings representing the five other New England states, will welcome visitors throughout the 17-day Eastern States Exposition, September 18 through October 4, 2026, in West Springfield, Massachusetts. Maine Day will be celebrated on Saturday, September 19.

For more than a century, the Maine Building has introduced generations of fairgoers to the people, products, and traditions that make Maine stand apart. The Maine Department of Agriculture, Conservation and Forestry (DACF) owns and operates the building as a showcase for Maine agriculture, food, fisheries, forests, tourism, artisans, and businesses.

"The Big E gives Maine a special opportunity to showcase our food, farms, and agricultural businesses to people from across New England and beyond," said DACF Commissioner Amanda Beal. "Food is one of the most immediate and memorable ways to make that connection. Someone may come into the Maine Building for a baked potato, lobster roll, or a maple or wild blueberry dish, but they leave with a greater appreciation for the farmers, producers, and small businesses behind those products."

The Big E is one of the largest fairs in North America, providing Maine businesses with access to an enormous regional marketplace. For exhibiting producers and makers, the opportunity extends beyond sales during the fair, helping introduce their products to new customers and build awareness that can lead to future visits, online purchases, and other business opportunities.

"We view the Big E as both a marketplace and a long-term opportunity to build awareness of Maine agriculture," said DACF Bureau of Agriculture, Food and Rural Resources Director Craig Lapine. "Many of Maine's farms and food businesses are small businesses, and reaching an audience of this scale is difficult to accomplish individually. By bringing them together in the Maine Building, we can show visitors the robust diversity of what Maine grows, harvests, makes and creates."

Taste Maine at The Big E

Food remains one of the biggest draws at the Maine Building, and the 2026 lineup offers fairgoers plenty of ways to experience Maine.

Longtime favorites include the Maine Potato Board's iconic loaded baked potatoes and Maine lobster rolls. Tree of Life Maple Farm will offer organic Maine maple syrup, maple cream, candy, cotton candy, coffee, and milkshakes, while Valley View Orchard Pies brings fruit pies, whoopie pies, and other baked goods from its Oxford bakery.

Maine aquaculture is also on the menu, with the Maine Aquaculture Association offering smoked salmon while introducing visitors to Maine's growing aquaculture sector and the Maine Oyster Trail.

This year's offerings also highlight collaborations among Maine farms and food businesses.

Fields Fields Blueberries, a woman-owned organic wild blueberry farm in Dresden, will serve its renowned wild blueberry crisp topped with Maine-made Gifford's ice cream.

QP Burger Food Truck will bring together products from multiple Maine businesses in its burgers, hot dogs, and sides, including Fox Family Potato Chips, Raye's Mustard, and Morse's sauerkraut.

Fire & Company Catering will showcase Maine flavors through wood-fired pizza and beverages featuring Maine producers and ingredients.

"These collaborations tell an important story about Maine's food economy," Beal said. "When Maine farms, food producers, and businesses use and promote one another's products, the benefit reaches beyond a single business. Visitors get a great Maine experience while seeing firsthand how interconnected our agricultural and food community can be."

More Than Food

The Maine Building experience extends well beyond the menu.

Visitors can shop for Maine-made wood products, jewelry, personal-care products, artisan goods, and gifts. Dailey Woodworking and Friends will feature work from more than a dozen Maine makers, alongside longtime and returning exhibitors including Ledgeway Farm, MARTINI Jewels, Sider's Woodcrafting, Sunshine Apothecary, and Winter Whimsies.

Short-term exhibitors rotating through the building include Maine authors and makers, Liberty Graphics, Pussums Cat Company, Sweet Monkey Business, and West Maquoit Vinegar Works.

The Maine Flower Collective will greet visitors with a display of Maine-grown dried flowers highlighting the state's flower farmers and florists, while the Maine Forest and Logging Museum will help tell the story of Maine's forestry heritage.

The Maine Office of Tourism will also be on hand, along with the Maine Tourism Association, to help visitors discover Maine destinations and experiences.

"Our goal is to spark a connection with Maine that inspires a visit to our state for culinary experiences," said Maine Office of Tourism Director Carolann Ouellette. "The Maine-made products on exhibit at the Big E all tell a story that is shaped by the landscape and culture of Maine. When fair attendees discover a Maine product, they get to learn about the farm and people behind the product, and that develops a bond that we hope will carry forward in a trip to Maine's farms and food businesses.

entry.content:
Wednesday, September 9, 2026

Jury Scam Alert

 

The U.S. District Court for the District of Maine is aware of an ongoing jury scam involving fraudulent text messages and emails claiming that recipients failed to report for jury duty.  These messages falsely use the name of “Judge Nye” or other court officials. 

These messages are not from the Court.  The Court will never send a text or email threatening arrest or demanding payment for missed jury service.

Do not respond, provide personal or financial information, click links, or send payment in response to these messages.  Jury Scams can be reported to Federal Trade Commission at ReportFraud.ftc.gov.

entry.content: The Exxon Mobil Corporation (Exxon) seeks a determination that Federal law preempts State common law claims brought against it in New Jersey concerning the safe transportation of gasoline in commerce. PHMSA is issuing a final administrative determination concluding that the State common law tort claims presented by Exxon are preempted. Each of these duties, if imposed, would present an obstacle to compliance with the Federal regulatory framework essential for the safe transportation of gasoline. In addition, any claims about covered subjects, such as the marking, loading and unloading, and classification of gasoline that are not substantively the same as the applicable HMR provisions are preempted.

Registration is Open for the 2026 MaineCare Provider Conference

Sep 10, 2026

Join colleagues from across Maine for the inaugural 2026 MaineCare Provider Conference—a dynamic day of learning, collaboration, and connection. Centered on the theme "Stronger Together: Navigating Change Through Collaboration," this conference brings together providers from across the MaineCare community to share innovative practices, explore emerging challenges, and strengthen partnerships that improve care for the people we serve. 

This conference is made possible through support from Maine's Rural Health Transformation Program (RHTP), a federal initiative that helps strengthen rural healthcare by improving access to care, supporting the healthcare workforce, modernizing healthcare systems, and advancing innovative models of care across the state. The conference reflects these goals by creating opportunities for providers to learn from one another, build stronger partnerships, and share strategies that improve care for MaineCare members. 

Designed for professionals across primary care, behavioral health, oral health, community support services, and other disciplines, the conference features interactive presentations, practical strategies, and real-world solutions that participants can immediately apply in their work. Whether you're looking to expand your knowledge, exchange ideas with peers, or build new connections across Maine's healthcare and social service systems, this conference offers valuable opportunities to learn from one another and shape the future of care. 

The conference welcomes participants in all roles with MaineCare provider organizations, including: 

  • Clinicians 
  • Administrators 
  • Care coordinators 
  • Program staff 
  • Quality improvement professionals 
  • Other team members who support MaineCare members 

Together, we'll explore approaches that strengthen the healthcare workforce, improve access to care, enhance member engagement, and support better health outcomes for MaineCare members across the state. 

Provider Conference Details 

Date: October 27, 2026 

Time: 9:00 AM – 3:00 PM (Registration, Poster Session, and Networking time begins at 8:00 AM) 

Place: Augusta Civic Center, Community Drive, Augusta, ME 

Cost: Free!  

Space is limited, so register now!  

Some Providers Are Required to Participate – See the Special Code 

If you are a Delivery System Reform Unit (DSRU) provider including: 

  • Behavioral Health Homes 
  • Certified Community Behavioral Health Clinics 
  • Community Care Teams 
  • MaineMOM 
  • Opioid Health Homes 
  • Primary Care Plus 

MaineCare policy requires at least one member of your care team to attend this department-sponsored learning activity.  

The registration code specifically designated for DSRU providers to help account for required participation is DSRUPROVIDER. Click the “reserve a spot” button on the registration page, and enter this code into the promo code box, to ensure you can access the reserved DSRU tickets. 

For questions about this conference, please contact MaineCare’s communication team.

Supreme Judicial Court Chief Justice Valerie Stanfill and members of the Supreme Judicial Court will conduct a student-teacher town hall on Thursday, September 17, 2026, to commemorate the 239th anniversary of the signing of the U.S. Constitution.

"The Constitution is the bedrock and framework of American democracy," said Chief Justice Stanfill. entry.title: Maine Wasted Food Prevention Week - September 28 through October 4 — Governor of Maine — Official Documents (Executive Orders)
entry.content:
WHEREAS, food is one of Maine’s most valuable resources and is essential for the health and nutrition of all our 1.4 million residents; and

WHEREAS, nearly 40 percent of food produced in Maine is never eaten – over 361,000 tons annually – primarily ending up in landfills where it produces dangerous methane gas which is 28 times more potent than carbon dioxide and a major contributor to climate change; and

WHEREAS, Maine people can save money by preventing wasted food, with the average Maine family spending nearly $3,000 annually on food that is thrown away; and

WHEREAS, over 80 percent of consumers misunderstand food date labels causing large amounts of perfectly good food to be thrown away in homes, businesses, and even food pantries; and

WHEREAS, Maine communities can substantially reduce their waste disposal costs by preventing wasted food since food is the single largest municipal solid waste component; and

WHEREAS, Maine K-12 schools have a special role in educating our next generation to reduce, recover, and recycle the estimated 7 million pounds of school food wasted annually; and

WHEREAS, we can help our farmers, strengthen our local food systems, and conserve our natural resources – water, air, energy, and land – by valuing Maine food and composting food scraps instead of wasting it as trash; 

NOW THEREFORE, be it resolved that I, Janet T. Mills, Governor of the State of Maine, do hereby proclaim the week of September 28-October 4, 2026, as

Maine Wasted Food Prevention Week

and I encourage all Maine people to become aware of the wasted food in our homes, schools and all around us, and to commit to stop throwing food away.

In testimony whereof, I have caused 
the Great Seal of the State to be 
hereunto affixed GIVEN under my 
hand at Augusta this second day 
of September Two Thousand Twenty-Six

entry.title: LGBTQ Veterans Day - September 20 — Governor of Maine — Official Documents (Executive Orders)

entry.title: First Responders Day - September 11 — Governor of Maine — Official Documents (Executive Orders)
entry.content:
WHEREAS, first responders include firefighters, police officers, nurses, paramedics, emergency medical services personnel, 911 dispatchers, search and rescue teams, and members of other organizations in the public safety sector; and

WHEREAS, 25 years ago, our Nation experienced the deadliest terrorist attack in its history when terrorists hijacked four civilian aircraft and crashed two of them into the World Trade Center in New York, one into the Pentagon outside Washington, D.C., and a fourth in southwestern Pennsylvania after passengers attempted to regain control of the aircraft from the hijackers and successfully managed to keep the plane from crashing in the Capital; and

WHEREAS, during one of our Nation’s most shocking and difficult times, first responders rushed directly to the scenes of the attacks, risking their lives while displaying incredible bravery and heroism to help as many people as possible; and

WHEREAS, 2,977 innocent lives were lost on September 11, 2001, including 6 Maine residents, 343 firefighters and 72 law enforcement officers; and

WHEREAS, on October 25th, 2023, our state experienced its worst mass casualty incident in Lewiston, where 18 innocent victims lost their lives and 13 more were injured; and

WHEREAS, in our most trying time, first responders rushed to the scenes of the crime to assist victims and find the perpetrator; and

WHEREAS, on that day and every day, Maine’s first responders risk their lives to protect us, serving as our first defense against emergencies that threaten our communities; and

WHEREAS, on this day, we honor Maine and the Nation’s brave, selfless, and compassionate heroes who save countless lives every day and pay tribute to those who have paid the ultimate price in the line of duty; and

WHEREAS, in accordance with 1 MRSA §150-P, the State of Maine observes First Responders Day on September 11 of each year; 

NOW THEREFORE, be it resolved that I, Janet T. Mills, Governor of the State of Maine, do hereby proclaim September 11, 2026 as 

First Responders Day

in Maine, and I urge all citizens to honor the tremendous sacrifices our first responders make to protect us all. 

In testimony whereof, I have caused

the Great Seal of the State to be

hereunto affixed GIVEN under my

hand at Augusta this second day 
of September Two Thousand Twenty-Six

entry.title: Honoring the Victims and Survivors of the September 11 Attacks — Governor of Maine — Newsroom Press Releases
entry.content:
Hello, this is Governor Janet Mills, and thank you for listening.

Robert and Jackie Norton's son was waiting for them in California 25 years ago. He was about to get married, but his parents, a retired couple from Lubec, never made it to the ceremony. Their plane, American Airlines Flight 11, hit the North Tower of the World Trade Center in a horrific act of terrorism on September 11, 2001.

Katie Ward, the sister of Stephen Ward, said her brother couldn't wait to take over the big city when he moved to New York. A native of Gorham, Maine, Stephen had big plans, and he encouraged everyone to go after what they wanted and live their best lives. Stephen was working on the 101st floor of the North Tower at the World Trade Center that fateful day.

Robert Jalbert was raised in Lewiston and lived in Swampscott, Massachusetts, when he boarded United Flight 175 for a business trip to California. People described him as an easygoing guy, a good friend, and a proud father who went to church every Sunday and served as a Eucharistic Minister. His flight struck the South Tower of the World Trade Center.

Attorney Jim Roux of Portland, someone who loved hiking Mount Washington. He was also on United Flight 175. Through this Saturday, September 12th, the summit of Mount Washington will be lit by two pillars of light that will be visible from 100 miles away to honor Jim Roux and the thousands of others whose lives were cut short that day.

Commander Robert Schlegel was a devoted husband, a decorated officer, and an avid ice hockey and football player. Originally from Gray, Maine, Commander Schlegel had been awarded the Purple Heart and other medals for his career-long service in the U.S. Navy. He had been promoted just a month before he boarded American Airlines Flight 77, which was then flown into the Pentagon, killing all on board.

25 years ago, Maine and the nation were forever changed by the September 11th terrorist attacks. On this solemn anniversary, I join the Maine people in pausing to remember the nearly 3,000 souls taken from us that day, including the six beloved people from Maine. And in saluting the courageous first responders who rushed towards danger, including those heroes still living with devastating health conditions caused by exposure to toxic flames and fumes.

One of those firefighters moved to Falmouth, Maine. Kevin Hogan wasn't working on September 11, but when the first plane struck the World Trade Center, he jumped into a pickup truck, heading to Ground Zero. Through a storm of ash, he and other firefighters searched for scraps of clothing and under rubble, praying to find and return loved ones to their families. So today, we recognize first responders like Kevin, and we also thank the many servicemembers who stepped up to keep our nation safe then and in the years since.

And we thank our friends in other countries who stood by us. On September 11, more than 250 flights were forced to divert to Canada, including 38 commercial flights that touched down in Gander, Newfoundland, when more than 7,000 passengers were stranded. A local TV station put out a call to "lend a hand, do what you can," and residents opened their homes to Americans in need. Now, more than ever before, we should remember that kindness of our neighbors to the North. 

Although more than a hundred million Americans are too young to remember that dark day, today, we take a moment to remember and to honor those who perished that day, as well as the first responders who ran towards danger and stayed through the devastating aftermath, and the men and women who stepped up and who continue to step up to keep us safe.

This is Governor Janet Mills, and on behalf of the 1.4 million people of the state of Maine, we honor those who perished, those who helped, those who stood by us, 25 years ago, September 11, 2001.
